before.label: Environmental history
before.description: Explains historical relations among people and the nonhuman world through ecological exchange, agriculture, property, commodity flows, conservation and cultural ideas of nature. These approaches disagree about causal emphasis. Cases from New England, the Great Plains, Mexico, India, colonial islands and South Africa connect ecological processes with power without supplying one universal model. Bullard’s environmental-justice inquiry and Rita and Jackie Huggins’s situated life histories broaden comparison toward unequal burdens, displacement and authority over historical accounts. Dust Bowl debates distinguish agricultural capitalism, technology and soils, federal intervention, regional scale and household survival; primary criticism and later social history complicate a single causal summary.
before.representative_figures_and_works: Alfred Crosby; Donald Worster; Carolyn Merchant; William Cronon. ASEH founded 1977. Expanded contextual readings include Leopold’s precursor essays, Melville’s Mexican study, Gadgil and Guha’s Indian history, Grove’s colonial conservation and Carruthers’s South African park history.

before.scope_note: Ecological exchange, political economy, and feminist critiques of nature overlap; institutional society history does not document every intellectual route. Crosby’s temperate-settler argument differs from Melville’s Mexican case; Gadgil and Guha’s resource conflicts differ from Grove’s conservation networks and Carruthers’s park politics. Cronon’s cultural account of wilderness does not deny nonhuman nature. The selection remains incomplete, especially in environmental justice and Indigenous scholarship. A bounded second-pass addition now compares Bullard and the Huggins collaboration; primary-excerpt, publisher-description and metadata limits remain distinct, and neither selection represents every community.

strands.title: Agricultural culture, technology and regional causes

strands.focus: Compare McDean’s insistence on a specific Dust Bowl region, Fite’s call for northern Plains coverage, and Riney-Kehrberg’s household survival study in southwestern Kansas. Causal explanation, geographical scale and lived experience pose different questions.

strands.title: Wilderness, livelihood and different political contexts
strands.focus: Guha targets American deep ecology’s universal claims and conservation’s unequal costs in India, while acknowledging Naess’s concern about inequality. Cronon studies American sublime/frontier ideals and everyday responsibility, explicitly citing Guha in note28. Shared concerns about exclusion do not erase their different contexts or Cronon’s support for protected wild lands.

strands.title: Can biocentrism incorporate social criticism?
strands.focus: Johns’s abstract disputes Guha’s equation of deep ecology with wilderness protection and defends biocentrism joined to critical social theory against overconsumption and militarism. This is a named response; the article’s detailed reasoning is not newly verified.

strands.title: Cultural criticism and habitat protection
strands.focus: Sessions objects that Cronon underweights biodiversity and connected wild habitat. His claim that cultural construction conflicts with independent nature is a critical interpretation: Cronon explicitly defends nonhuman autonomy and wild-land protection.

before.label: Postcolonial history / critique
before.description: Questions imperial knowledge, Eurocentric universals, and the assumption that all societies follow Europe’s historical path.

before.scope_note: Said, Spivak, and Chakrabarty address different problems; literary critique and historical scholarship interact without becoming the same discipline. Feminist critiques, colonial archival research and theories of ambivalence introduce further disagreements. These selections do not make postcolonial thought synonymous with South Asian history, literary theory or all anti-colonial politics.

The page identifies the 1995 chapter. The argument is not that nonhuman nature is simply invented; reception and critics remain a follow-up.

outcomes.finding: Guha’s1989 critique and Cronon’s1995 essay now have differentiated contextual treatment, including Cronon’s direct citation of Guha. Johns’s1990 abstract and Sessions’s1996 primary response introduce named counterarguments. Inden’s specific analytical contribution to Guha supplies a documented cross-group route.
outcomes.research_limit: Complete Guha PDF text and author-hosted Cronon reflow/notes traversed with transcription errors; no full image collation. Cronon note28 checked against1996 journal text to correct reflow’s misrendered Guha surname. Johns author abstract and metadata only, direct record/DOI fetch failed. Sessions full journal HTML read as polemical reception, not neutral evidence about all environmentalists or postmodernists. Cronon’s separate1996 response metadata checked, body inaccessible and not used. Inden original and empirical conservation cases unread. Selected responses resolve the bounded comparison; no exhaustive reception claim.
